Welcome to the Delta Simulations Documentation Hub, for any and all information about our projects

You Should Know

The documentation provided is a Work in Progress, and may feature incomplete information. Please refer to our Discord for the most up-to-date information.

    The UH-60 Blackhawk is a four-bladed, twin-engine, medium-lift utility helicopter manufactured by Sikorsky Aircraft.

  • C-17A Globemaster III Documentation Coming Soon

    The C-17A Globemaster III is a large military transport aircraft developed by McDonnell Douglas (now Boeing). It's capable of rapid strategic delivery of troops and cargo to main operating bases or forward operating bases.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If the above methods do not work:

To find the Community folder that MSFS is using, please follow these steps:

  1. Go to your General Settings in MSFS and activate Developer Mode.
  2. Go to the menu and select 'Virtual File System'.
  3. Click on 'Packages Folders' and select 'Open Community Folder'. This opens the Community folder in a Windows Explorer. Please ensure that your add-ons are installed in the folder that is opened.

docs.title: How do I report an issue?
docs.text:
CHECK THIS FIRST

We highly recommend joining Our Discord for the fastest response time. Alternatively, please submit a Github Issue on the relevant repo containing the aircraft version, simulator version, and specific, reproducible steps to achieve this issue. Please be as specific as possible.

docs.title: Before Reporting Issues
docs.text:
Please try removing all other mods/liveries from the community folder and test our add-on again. We also reccomend doing a clean install. This will help rule out conflicts.

Most reported issues are caused by conflicts with other mods and liveries, or from an incorrect installation. If this does not resolve your issue, please continue below.

docs.title: How Can I Support Development?
docs.text:
If you are looking to assist with the development, you can start immediately with a PR or fork on our Github, though we highly recommend first filling out our Team Application Form so we can onboard you onto our server, and you can gain access to our reference libraries.

As a freeware organization, we rely on self-funding to cover the software, equipment, and subscriptions required to develop our projects. After years of development and thousands of dollars personally invested, we’re working to make the group more sustainable for the long term.

Donations are the most effective way to support our work if you are not a developer:

Donate via PayPal

Supporters receive a special role on our Discord server along with sneak peeks and additional updates on our development progress. If you donate, please contact a moderator on Discord with proof of donation to receive your role.

Please note: donations do not provide early access to any of our projects — only additional development updates and behind-the-scenes information.

docs.title: Will These Projects Be Available on Xbox?
docs.text: These projects are PC-only at this time, and will remain so for the foreseable future.

docs.title: When I Click a Button/Test, It Doesn't Work as it Should
docs.text: Our aircraft code runs on the PC-based XML scripting which is much easier to debug and adapt for complex aircraft. As a result, you may run into interaction issues when using the XBOX/LOCK control modes. We design our aircraft for use in the LEGACY control mode

docs.title: Are These Projects Free?
docs.text: Yes! This is the heart of our philosophy - our aircrafts will forever be free, open-source, and available to all. We will never gatekeep products behind paywalls or limited access. What you see is what you get.

docs.title: When is the Next Update?
docs.text: We are a team of volunteers developing in our free time and are thus unable to provide an estimate for a release date. We believe in releasing "beta" test builds of our aircraft, allowing for an effective feedback loop. When we believe we have a stable enough build, we will post it in our Discord, and it will be available on Github under the aircraft's releases. Then, you can follow our download instructions available above.

docs.title: Welcome to the UH-60M
docs.text: Welcome to the UH-60M Blackhawk documentation for Delta Simulations. This guide will help you understand the aircraft systems, flight controls, and operational procedures.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
WARNING

FOR SIMULATION USE ONLY

This documentation is intended for simulation purposes only, for use exclusively with the Delta Simulations UH-60M. This is not to be used in the real world.

Work in Progress

This documentation is an active work in progress, and is subject to change. Please report any issues on our Github, or on the Delta Simulations Discord Server.

The UH-60M Black Hawk is a medium-lift utility helicopter used for transport, medical evacuation, and special operations. This guide will help you learn the systems, features, and abilities this aircraft has.

We have simulated several variants of this aircraft, covering military to civilian uses.** All Simulated Variants**

To learn more, troubleshoot issues, and connect with our community, please join our Discord

Join our Discord

docs.title: Cockpit Displays
docs.text:
Use the keys around the edge of a multifunction display to select a page.

Page What you'll find PFD — Primary Flight Display Attitude, airspeed, altitude and heading. ND — Navigation Display Navigation information. EICAS — Engine Instrument Caution/Advisory System Engine and rotor indications, cautions and advisories. TAC — Tactical Map A map view. JVMF — Joint Variable Message Format The mission data page used during cockpit setup.

The MFD page list also lists IVHMS, the vehicle health monitoring page, as coming soon.

docs.title: Batteries and generators
docs.text: The batteries provide power before a generator is online. On the overhead panel, BATT NO. 1 and BATT NO. 2 control the batteries. The two engine generators and the APU generator each have a separate switch.

docs.title: Flight control hydraulics
docs.text:
Hydraulic pressure assists the flight controls. The BACKUP HYD PUMP switch belongs to the hydraulic system. The nearby fuel pump switches serve the engines and APU.

The Before Start checklist gives the initial switch positions. The Cockpit Equipment Checks cover the next part of the startup.

docs.title: Cyclic, Collective and Pedals
docs.text:
Set up these axes in your MSFS helicopter controls profile. The pilot and copilot have the same primary controls.

Cockpit control Axis What it does Cyclic Pitch and roll Tilts the rotor disc forward, aft, left or right. Collective Collective Changes the pitch of all main rotor blades together. Pedals Yaw Changes tail rotor thrust to swing the nose left or right.

Move one control at a time and watch the matching control in the cockpit. If the nose turns the wrong way when you press a pedal, check the direction of the yaw axis in your profile.

SAS is the stability augmentation system. It damps unwanted motion. You'll also see TRIM and FPS (flight path stabilization) in the cockpit equipment checks.

docs.title: Engines, Fuel and APU
docs.text: The UH-60M has two T700-GE-701D turboshaft engines. Select EICAS on a multifunction display to see the engine and rotor indications together.

docs.title: Fuel system
docs.text: The helicopter carries fuel in two main tanks. Each engine has its own fuel feed. On the overhead panel, the engine boost pump switches are separate from the FUEL PUMP selector used for APU boost.

docs.title: Auxiliary power unit
docs.text:
The APU supplies electrical power on the ground and bleed air for engine start. The APU CONT switch controls the unit. The APU generator switch controls its electrical output.

For the switch sequence in the sim, see Starting Engines.

docs.title: Cabin Heating and Ventilation
docs.text: Several controls can affect airflow in a UH-60M cockpit. The HEATER changes the temperature of the air sent through the ducts. The VENT BLOWER circulates ambient air. Adjustable nozzles near the consoles let the pilots direct ram air where they want it.

docs.title: Heat source and airflow
docs.text:
The basic heating system mixes outside air with hot compressed air taken from an engine compressor. The latter is called bleed air. The APU can also supply it on the ground. The mixing system regulates the temperature delivered to the cabin and cockpit outlets. By contrast, the electric ventilation blower moves ambient air through the cabin ducts even when no heat is selected.

The AIR SCE HT/STRT label in Delta's Before Start checklist means air source for heat and start. The selector identifies the pneumatic source. The separate heater control sets the heat delivered to the occupants. This explains why the air-source selector also appears in the add-on's engine runup checklist.

docs.title: Cabin equipment varies
docs.text:
The manual describes more than one cabin installation. An AUX CABIN HEATER panel refers to supplemental cabin heat. The environmental control system (ECS) described for a medical cabin recirculates air and can cool it using an electrically driven refrigeration system. A panel near the rear medic seat controls that installation.

The documented simulator interaction is the air-source selector in the linked checklists. The auxiliary heater, rear-cabin ECS and temperature response depend on what the selected add-on variant implements.

Manual reference: TM 1-1520-280-10, Chapter 2, Section X, paragraphs 2-55 through 2-59.

docs.title: Main and Tail Rotors
docs.text: Two details to look for in an exterior view are the four blades above the cabin and the angle of the tail rotor. On the UH-60M, both rotors receive power from the transmission, and each changes blade pitch in response to the flight controls.

docs.title: Main rotor head
docs.text:
The four main blades meet at a central hub. Pitch is the angle of a blade about its long axis. The swashplate and pitch links change that angle as the blades turn. The hub also lets each blade move up or down (flap) and move slightly forward or back in the plane of rotation (lead or lag). These are different motions from changing blade pitch.

When the rotor is stationary, droop stops support the blades. This accounts for the difference in blade position between a parked aircraft and one carrying its weight on the rotor. The manual also describes a vibration absorber at the rotor head that limits the vibration passed into the fuselage.

docs.title: Tail rotor
docs.text: The tail rotor sits on the right side of the raised tail pylon. The tilt is intentional. Most of its thrust acts sideways to counter the turning effect of the main rotor and control yaw. Because its thrust is angled, a part of it also supports the helicopter's weight in a hover.

docs.title: Vibration in the cockpit
docs.text:
The airframe has a separate active vibration control system. It senses rotor-induced vibration in the aircraft and generates an opposing vibration. The VIB CONT switch in Delta's Before Start checklist refers to this system. The checklist identifies the cockpit control. Camera shake or force feedback alone cannot tell you how much of the system your add-on models.

Manual reference: TM 1-1520-280-10, Chapter 2, Section VIII, paragraphs 2-45 through 2-47, and Section IX, paragraph 2-54.

docs.title: Standby Flight Instruments
docs.text: The Electronic Standby Instrument System (ESIS) gives the pilots a compact second view of the aircraft's attitude and motion. In the UH-60M described by the manual, it has a dedicated display, air data computer, magnetic sensor and backup battery. It can display pitch, roll, airspeed, altitude, vertical speed and heading independently of the selected multifunction display page.

docs.title: Read the standby picture
docs.text: Indication How to interpret it Attitude The fixed aircraft reference and moving horizon show pitch and bank. The roll pointer reads against the scale above them. Airspeed, altitude and vertical speed The standby air data computer uses pressure from the pitot-static system. The BARO setting provides the pressure reference for displayed altitude. When comparing the main and standby altitudes in the sim, first check that their pressure settings match. Heading Read the heading tape at its fixed center index. The standby system has a magnetic sensor to supply this information.

docs.title: Other visual references
docs.text: The manual places a separate magnetic compass on the right center windshield frame above the instrument panel. A panel clock offers clock time (C) and elapsed time (ET). Two direct-reading indicators in the overhead windows show outside air temperature in degrees Celsius. These references can help identify instruments in cockpit views where only their labels are legible.

docs.title: The add-on's standby check
docs.text:
Delta's Before Start checklist identifies the battery check indication as BATT GOOD and calls out the ESIS tone during the standby instrument check. The Cockpit Equipment Checks list the STBY INST switch again. These are the cues the developer documents for the add-on. The manual's instrument layout gives context for identifying the remaining indications.

Manual reference: TM 1-1520-280-10, Chapter 2, Section XIV, paragraphs 2-69, 2-70 and 2-75 through 2-77.

docs.title: Transmission and Tail Drive
docs.text: The UH-60M has two engines and one main rotor. Each engine feeds its own input module on the main transmission above the cabin. The main transmission brings the two inputs together, reduces their speed and turns the main rotor mast. A second drive takes power aft to the tail rotor.

docs.title: Follow the power through the aircraft
docs.text: Component What it drives Main transmission The main rotor above the cabin and the drive shaft leading into the tail. Accessory modules A generator and a hydraulic pump on each side. This mechanical connection helps explain why generator indications change as the rotor comes up to speed. Intermediate gearbox The next section of the tail drive at the bend near the base of the tail pylon. Tail gearbox The tail rotor at the top of the pylon. Its gears turn the drive through the final change in direction.

docs.title: Read the indications
docs.text:
In the add-on's engine runup checklist, Q1 and Q2 refer to the torque supplied by each engine. NR refers to the speed of their shared main rotor. Two torque indications and one rotor speed are what you would expect from this arrangement.

XMSN on a cockpit label stands for transmission. In the aircraft manual, MAIN XMSN oil temperature and pressure describe the lubricant circulating through the main gearbox. Engine oil belongs to a separate system. Delta's published checklist documents the torque, rotor speed and generator cues. The gearbox description here explains their mechanical context.

Manual reference: TM 1-1520-280-10, Chapter 2, Section VII, paragraphs 2-42 through 2-44.

docs.title: Windshield and Pitot Heat
docs.text:
The windshield wipers, heated glass and heated pitot probes serve three different purposes. A wiper clears water that is already on the glass. Windshield heat acts on the glass itself. Pitot heat acts on the external probes that supply pressure information to the flight instruments.

Cockpit label in the aircraft manual What it refers to WINDSHIELD WIPER One motor drives a wiper on each pilot's windshield. LOW and HI select wiping speeds. OFF stops the blades where they are. PARK returns them to the inboard windshield frames. WINDSHIELD ANTI-ICE Transparent electrical conductors heat the glass for anti-icing and defogging. The pilot, copilot and center panes have individual switches. The center pane can therefore have its own heat control even though it has no wiper. PITOT HEAT Heating elements in the external pitot probes help keep their pressure openings clear of ice. The two probes sit behind and above the cockpit doors.

A moving wiper is a visible mechanical effect. Pitot heat has no comparable effect on the windshield. If you're looking around the virtual cockpit, the separate controls explain why a clear windshield tells you little about what the probes are sensing. For the instruments that use those pressure inputs, see Standby Flight Instruments.

These labels and switch positions describe the aircraft in the manual. The add-on's published cockpit checklists do not establish which glass-heating, wiper-parking or probe-icing effects are simulated.

Manual reference: TM 1-1520-280-10, Chapter 2, Section IX, paragraphs 2-49 and 2-50, and Section XIV, paragraph 2-69.

docs.title: Axis Calibration and Troubleshooting
docs.text: With the H-60 parked, check each physical axis before adjusting how the helicopter handles. Open Controls, select the device, then open Hardware settings for that axis. Watch its input indicator as you move the control. Make a copy of your usual profile first if you're experimenting with response curves.

docs.title: Centre, direction and travel
docs.text:
1. Check the centre. Rest a spring-centred stick or the pedals and take your hands or feet off. If the indicator jitters, add a small centre dead zone and observe the same input again. Stop increasing the dead zone once the jitter disappears. A collective or throttle lever can rest anywhere in its travel and has no equivalent spring centre.
  2. Check each direction. Move fore and aft with the stick held close to centre on the other axis. Then repeat left and right. If the wrong axis responds, correct the assignment. If the correct axis responds backwards in the cockpit, reverse that axis.
  3. Check the ends. Move through the full stroke slowly. The indicator should change smoothly. A gap in the middle and a shortfall at the end are different problems. Compare the reading with the device's own calibration screen before changing the response curve.
  4. Check with all your devices connected. Move one control while leaving the others still. If the input jumps back to another position, inspect the bindings on the second device as well. This is easy to miss with a gamepad left connected beside a HOTAS.

docs.title: Common symptoms
docs.text:
What you see What to check Twisting the stick changes the nose direction even though pedals are connected Look for a yaw or tail rotor binding on both devices. Clear the one you aren't using in the active profile. Moving the quadrant changes a throttle lever while the collective stays put Search by that physical input and check whether it is assigned to helicopter throttle, collective, or both. The cyclic barely responds around centre, then moves suddenly Compare the physical input indicator with the response curve. A large dead zone uses up part of the available travel. A button changes the control a little at a time Check whether an increment or decrement command was chosen in place of an axis. A change worked yesterday but has disappeared Select the H-60 and check the active profile on the actual device. The stick and quadrant can each have a different profile selected.

For small adjustments, change one setting and repeat the same movement. Start with direction and range, then adjust sensitivity until small movements feel manageable with your stick length and grip.

MSFS 2024 controller settings

docs.title: Cockpit and Cabin Lighting
docs.text: The cockpit has separate controls for backlit lettering, floodlights and the utility light at each seat. The cabin has its own colour selector. In a night flight, decide what you need to see first. If the lettering on the overhead is hard to read, raise the overhead backlight. If you need to see the shape of a switch or an unlit surface, use a flood or utility light.

docs.title: Panel illumination
docs.text:
Cockpit control or tooltip Area to watch OH PNL BACKLIGHT Overhead panel lettering INST PNL BACKLIGHT Instrument panel backlight LWR CSL BACKLIGHT Lower console, radio panels and collective lettering LIGHTED SWITCH INTENSITY Illumination of the lighted switches PILOT MASTER WARNING LIGHTING / COPILOT MASTER WARNING LIGHTING Master warning lighting on the selected side

The panel knobs above move in ten-percentage-point steps in version 5.2.4. One or two clicks at a time make it easier to balance adjacent panels. If the radios and collective labels are too bright while the overhead looks right, turn down LWR CSL BACKLIGHT and keep the overhead setting.

docs.title: Flood and utility lights
docs.text:
The cockpit floodlights cover a wider area. Their brightness knob has finer five-point steps. COCKPIT LIGHT COLOUR switches between the white and green floodlight effects. Colour and brightness are separate controls, so changing colour at zero brightness produces little to see.

Each seat also has UTIL LIGHT MODE and UTIL LIGHT POWER. Mode changes the colour of that seat's utility light. Power adjusts its intensity in twenty-point steps from off to full. If the other seat is lit and yours is dark, adjust the control for your side. This is a useful option when you want a little light at one seat without flooding the entire cockpit.

docs.title: Cabin lights
docs.text:
The cabin switch has three labeled positions, WHITE, OFF and BLUE. View the cabin behind the seats to see the change. The cockpit floodlight colour selector and utility light knobs affect the flight deck, so they can be left where you want them while changing the cabin lights for a passenger view or screenshot.

H-60 interior lighting controls · H-60 lighting circuits and effects

docs.title: Exterior Lights and Searchlight
docs.text: The H-60 has position lights, upper and lower anti-collision beacons, a landing light and a steerable searchlight. For a quick visual check, park near a patch of unlit pavement and use the external camera. It is easier to distinguish the two forward lamps when you can see both the fixture and where its beam lands.

docs.title: Position lights and beacons
docs.text: The position lights are red on the left, green on the right and white at the tail. Their selector is labeled NAV DIM, NAV OFF and NAV BRT. For the anti-collision lights, one switch selects UPPER, BOTH or LOWER. The other selects DAY, OFF or NIGHT. If one beacon is missing, check the first switch. If neither beacon is visible, check the second switch. The add-on uses different effects for the day and night settings.

docs.title: Landing light and searchlight
docs.text:
The cockpit has two individual push controls. Search Light CNTRL switches the steerable lamp. Landing Light CNTRL switches the landing lamp. When using generic lighting commands from a hardware panel, the searchlight uses the simulator's landing light channel and the landing lamp uses the taxi light channel. If your hardware switch operates the other lamp, try the labeled cockpit control to identify it first.

Four button assignments position the searchlight. The aircraft intercepts the following MSFS cowl flap commands, which explains their unusual names in a hardware profile.

Searchlight motion MSFS event Extend INC_COWL_FLAPS4 Retract DEC_COWL_FLAPS4 Left INC_COWL_FLAPS3 Right DEC_COWL_FLAPS3

The directional inputs move the fixture in small steps. With power available, extend the light several steps before checking left and right travel. At full retraction, the model returns the sideways aim to centre. If the lamp is lit but appears to ignore sideways commands, check that it has moved out of the stowed position. To confirm that a four-way hat is wired as intended, leave the helicopter stationary and move the beam across the same patch of pavement.

H-60 searchlight bindings · H-60 light controls · H-60 lighting logic

docs.title: Helicopter Controller Profiles
docs.text: In MSFS 2024, select the H-60 at the top of Settings → Controls, then select your stick, throttle quadrant or pedals from the device list. Each device has its own assignments. If you select the stick while trying to bind the pedals, the pedals won't appear in the assignment you're editing.

docs.title: Four axes for the H-60
docs.text:
Physical movement Search term Assignment Stick forward and back Cyclic longitudinal Pitch axis Stick left and right Cyclic lateral Roll axis Pedals, or the twist grip on a stick Tail rotor Yaw axis Collective lever, or one lever on a throttle quadrant Collective Collective axis

Choose the continuous axis command for each lever or stick movement. Commands such as increase, decrease, left and right apply a step each time you press a button. An analog axis sends its position throughout the travel. A throttle quadrant works as a collective once you assign its lever to collective. The separate helicopter throttle command operates a different control.

docs.title: Where to save a binding
docs.text:
Use the helicopter category profile for the axes you want to carry between helicopters. Use the H-60 model profile for its special controls, such as the searchlight. For example, its searchlight uses commands labeled as cowl flaps in the simulator. Keeping those assignments in the H-60 profile leaves the same buttons available for other aircraft.

To keep a working preset, use the gear next to its name to duplicate it. A name like H-60 – twist grip or H-60 – pedals makes it easier to switch between the two setups. If you have both a twist stick and pedals, give yaw to the device you plan to use on this flight.

docs.title: Finding a command
docs.text:
Set the filter to None when looking for an unassigned command. Assigned is useful once you want to review the bindings already on that device. To see what a specific physical input does, choose Search by input and move just that axis or press just that button. If a number appears beside a binding, open its gear to see the conflicting assignments.

MSFS 2024 controller settings · Helicopter axis commands

docs.title: Pilot Seats and Instrument Views
docs.text: The H-60 includes dedicated cockpit views for the primary flight display, multifunction display, overhead panel and pedestal. Use an instrument view when you need to read a small label or select a switch. Return to the pilot view for the normal windshield sightline.

docs.title: Choosing a view
docs.text:
View What it shows Pilot The standard forward view from the pilot seat. Use it as your reference after looking around. Landing pilot view A higher eye position angled down through the front of the cockpit. Useful for seeing more of the ground in front of the aircraft. Copilot The opposite seat. Useful for checking the other utility light or viewing a panel from the other side. PFD A close view of the primary flight display. MFD A close view of the multifunction display. Overhead The panel above the pilots. The preset aims upward and leaves your hands free to operate switches with the mouse. Pedestal The console between the seats. The preset looks down towards the controls and panel lettering.

A camera change only changes your viewpoint. Selecting the MFD view, for example, moves your eye in front of that display. Use the display's bezel keys to select the page you want to read. Overhead and Pedestal are instrument views too, even though they point at switches.

docs.title: Quick looks and cockpit access
docs.text:
The cockpit includes three quick looks to the left and three to the right, plus up and down views. A dedicated quick-look hat lets you glance towards a side window without slewing a free camera back into position. If you also assign a hat to the searchlight, check for conflicts so that moving the lamp doesn't turn your head at the same time.

The aircraft tablet has a click point labeled EFB HIDE/SHOW. Use it if the tablet obstructs your view, and use the corresponding mount click point to bring it back. A separate Pilot VR viewpoint provides the headset starting position. If you are adjusting an eye position on a monitor, select the ordinary pilot viewpoint before judging the result.

H-60 camera presets · Tablet visibility control

docs.title: Rotor Trim and Flight Assistance
docs.text: The H-60 has buttons labeled SAS 1, SAS 2, FPS and TRIM. MSFS also has controller commands with the word trim in their names. Which one you select matters, especially on a spring-centred stick.

docs.title: Controls in the aircraft
docs.text:
SAS stands for stability augmentation system. FPS stands for flight path stabilization. The H-60's cockpit equipment checks group the two SAS channels with FPS and trim. In the model, each of the four buttons toggles its own state. Pressing the cockpit control labeled TRIM RESET does something different. It sends the simulator's rotor trim reset command.

If you're following a checklist item that calls for the AFCS trim switch, look for AFCS TRIM. If you're testing a controller profile and need to clear a rotor trim offset, use TRIM RESET. Selecting the four AFCS buttons alone doesn't establish an altitude, heading or hover hold.

docs.title: Commands for a spring-centred stick
docs.text:
MSFS function Effect Longitudinal rotor trim Adjusts pitch trim fore or aft. Lateral rotor trim Adjusts roll trim left or right. Rotor trim reset Restores the default rotor trim values. Helicopter force trim release Holds the simulated cyclic position while you recentre a physical stick. Releasing the button reconnects the stick at the new reference.

For the MSFS force trim release function, use a momentary button you can hold and release. With the helicopter parked, move the stick off centre, hold the button, return the physical stick to centre, then release. This lets you check whether your control profile sends both the press and the release. A latching switch can leave the release command held. This is a simulator input function and does not require a force feedback base.

docs.title: Simulator assistance
docs.text:
MSFS 2024 lists Assisted cyclic, Assisted tail rotor and Assisted collective as separate piloting assists. When comparing how two profiles handle, use the same assistance settings for both flights. A pilot checking a new set of pedals, for example, can compare the same short flight with just the tail rotor assistance changed. That makes the effect easier to distinguish from a new yaw response curve.

H-60 cockpit controls · MSFS helicopter trim commands · MSFS piloting assists

docs.title: First Flight Cockpit Walkthrough
docs.text: For a first session with the Delta H-60, pick a familiar airport, daylight and clear weather. A parking spot gives you time to find the panels. A runway start can put the aircraft in a different state, so choose the same starting position if you repeat the flight.

docs.title: At the parking spot
docs.text:
1. Open the Before Start checklist. Find the parking brake, standby instrument switch and two battery switches before changing your cockpit view.
  2. Follow Cockpit Equipment Checks. When the displays come on, select a flight display on one screen and EICAS on another. That gives you a flight picture and an engine picture without changing pages.
  3. Use Starting Engines for the add-on's start and runup sequence. Watch the two engine-out indicators separately and note which clears first. Check the rotor indication on EICAS as the rotor accelerates.
  4. Set a view that shows the attitude display and enough of the windshield to see the horizon. Before leaving the parking area, confirm that you can reach that view again after using the overhead panel.

docs.title: A short local flight
docs.text:
Choose one nearby landmark and return to the same airport. On the outbound leg, compare heading on the flight display with your movement over the ground. If you have wind selected in MSFS, the direction the nose points and the track over the ground can differ.

On return, use the Landing and Parking and Shutdown pages. If something in the cockpit differed from the guide, note the aircraft version, variant, parking or runway start, panel label and indication. Those details make a repeat flight or a bug report much more useful than “startup didn't work.”

docs.title: Parking Brake and Tailwheel Lock
docs.text:
Two controls matter when the helicopter is sitting on its wheels. The parking brake holds the main wheels. The tailwheel lock controls whether the tailwheel can swivel. You can have a locked tailwheel and still roll forward.

Control Where to look in the cockpit What changes in MSFS Parking brake Handle with the tooltip SET/STOW PARKING BRAKE The handle follows the simulator's parking brake position. A click toggles the brake and plays an interior handle sound. Tailwheel lock Pushbutton with the tooltip TAIL WHEEL The button toggles the simulator's tailwheel lock. Its locked and unlocked indicators follow that state.

docs.title: Checking a controller binding
docs.text:
Start at a parking spot on level ground. With the helicopter stationary, click the parking brake handle once and note its position. Use your hardware parking brake command once. The handle should move back. If one press sets and immediately releases it, look for a second assignment on the same button or a controller sending a second toggle when you release the button.

Repeat the check with the TAIL WHEEL button and watch its indicator. Trying to judge the lock by turning the pedals while stationary can be misleading. The V5.2.4 flight model disables steering while stopped and sets the locked tailwheel's swivel range to zero.

docs.title: At the end of a flight
docs.text: The project's Landing checklist calls out both controls. The Parking and Shutdown checklist includes the parking brake and wheel chocks as separate items. If you come back to the sim after opening a menu, check the handle itself before assuming the brake is set.

docs.title: Warning Panel and Lamp Test
docs.text:
During a parking-spot start, a powered warning panel can show #1 ENG OUT, #2 ENG OUT and LOW ROTOR R.P.M. together. Delta's Cockpit Equipment Checks list this combination while the engines are still stopped.

Indication What drives the cockpit lamp in V5.2.4 #1 ENG OUT The simulator reports no combustion in engine 1. #2 ENG OUT The simulator reports no combustion in engine 2. The two lamps have separate inputs. LOW ROTOR R.P.M. The cockpit model flashes this lamp when simulated main rotor speed is below its programmed threshold. The lamp reads rotor speed independently of the two engine lamps.

docs.title: Reading the panel during startup
docs.text:
Watch what changes as the aircraft state changes. An engine lamp can clear while the rotor is still coming up to speed. The three lights tell you about two engines and one rotor, so they need not clear together. Use the engine instruments for the actual readings.

The button labeled LAMPS TEST in the checklist has the cockpit tooltip TEST ANNUN. A click toggles the lamp-test state in this version. If several lamps stay illuminated after you've checked them, click again to leave the test and read the panel under its normal conditions.

For a repeatable comparison, load the same variant at the same parking spot. Record the lights you see before startup and again after the sim's engine runup. Include the spawn state and whether lamp test was selected when reporting a panel discrepancy.

docs.title: Barometric and Radar Altitude
docs.text: The PFD has two altitude indications in feet. FEET is barometric altitude. RA is height over the terrain beneath the helicopter. Both can be correct while showing very different numbers.

docs.title: Barometric altitude
docs.text:
The large numbered dial uses the simulator's indicated altitude. Each full turn of the needle represents 1,000 feet. Read the digital window for the thousands as well as the hundreds. It moves in 10-foot steps. The pressure setting alongside the dial is marked IN, for inches of mercury.

For example, at an airport about 4,000 feet above sea level, the dial should read roughly 4,000 feet on the ground when the pressure setting matches the local altimeter setting. It will continue to read about 4,000 feet as you taxi across a level ramp.

docs.title: Radar altitude
docs.text:
At that same airport, RA should read near zero on the ground. In level flight, RA decreases as the ground rises beneath you even if barometric altitude holds steady. The navigation display also carries an RA readout, so you can check height above terrain while looking at the route.

Height over terrain in V5.2.4 RA indication Up to about 1,050 feet Dial and digital height. Above about 1,050 through 1,500 feet Digital height only. Above about 1,500 feet The RA dial and digital height drop out. Barometric altitude remains available on the PFD.

If the RA number disappears during a climb, check the height range before changing display settings. When crossing sloping terrain, use the vertical speed indication to check whether the helicopter itself is climbing or descending.

V5.2.4 instrument reference

docs.title: Cockpit Clock and Elapsed Time
docs.text:
The cockpit clock has a sweep seconds hand and two rows of digits. The top row shows hours and minutes on a 24-hour clock. The second row shows seconds. For example, 1437 above 08 reads 14:37:08. The letter at the bottom tells you which time you're looking at.

Mode What the digits show C Local time in the simulator. When recording a VATSIM time in UTC, account for the difference between local time and UTC. ET Elapsed hours, minutes and seconds. Use it to time a route leg or a hover exercise.

docs.title: Timing a leg
docs.text:
Use Clock Mode toggle to select ET. Clock Control cycles through run, stop and reset. With the timer reset at zero, press Clock Control as you pass the first waypoint. Press it again at the next waypoint to hold the reading. Read the result before pressing the control a third time to reset it.

If the time looks frozen, check the letter at the bottom. ET can hold a stopped time, while C follows the simulator clock. Switching between C and ET changes which time you see. A reset is a separate action on Clock Control.

V5.2.4 instrument reference

docs.title: Display Power and Bezel Keys
docs.text:
The keys along the bottom of each multifunction display select the page for that screen. Use the physical key directly under the label. The first three keys from the left are the ones you'll use most on an ordinary flight.

Bezel key Page Typical use PFD Primary Flight Display Fly by attitude, airspeed, heading and altitude. ND Navigation Display Follow the route and identify the next turn. EICAS Engine Instrument Caution/Advisory System Read engine and rotor indications, main fuel quantity and crew alerts.

You can keep the PFD in front of you and bring up EICAS on an adjacent screen during startup. Select ND on that same screen once you want the route back. The first screen stays on PFD.

docs.title: Power and brightness
docs.text:
Each display has its own PWR switch. The BK LT rocker adjusts a shared backlight setting, so the other screens can brighten or dim with it. Panel lighting controls the lettering around the displays separately.

If one screen is dark while the others are readable, check its PWR switch. If all the screens are dark after loading at a parking spot, follow the electrical setup in the Quick Start Guide. When the instruments first load, a solid color can cover the readouts for a few seconds.

On V5.2.4, a second press of EICAS from the engine page selects IVHMS. Press EICAS again to return to the engine instruments.

V5.2.4 instrument reference

docs.title: Engine and Rotor Indications
docs.text:
Select EICAS on the bottom bezel. The engine indications are grouped around the central rotor-speed indication. Read the label as well as the number. Several neighboring instruments use percentages but measure different things.

Label Quantity Units Q Engine torque Percent NG Gas generator speed Percent TGT Turbine gas temperature Degrees Celsius NP1, NP2 Power turbine speed for the numbered engine Percent NR Main rotor speed Percent Engine oil temperature and pressure Oil temperature and pressure for the engine Degrees Celsius and psi, respectively

The Q and NR indications answer different questions. Q shows how much torque an engine is delivering. NR shows how fast the rotor is turning. When comparing two screenshots or reporting an instrument issue, include the label and unit along with the reading.

docs.title: Comparing the engines
docs.text: V5.2.4 feeds both sets of EICAS engine tapes from engine 1. That includes torque, NG, TGT, NP, and oil temperature and pressure. The two sides can move together even when you change only one engine in the simulator. The Q1 and Q2 readouts on the PFD use separate engine torque inputs and offer another place to check what the sim is reporting.

docs.title: Fuel on EICAS
docs.text:
The MAIN FUEL indications show tank 1 and tank 2 by weight in pounds. TOTAL uses the simulator's total fuel weight. Each number rounds down to the nearest five pounds, so the two displayed tank values can add up to slightly less than the displayed total even with only the main tanks aboard.

V5.2.4 instrument reference

docs.title: Navigation Display and Flight Plan
docs.text: Select ND on the bottom bezel. The helicopter symbol sits in the circular map area. The boxed number at the top gives current gyro heading in degrees. The short marks around the compass are five degrees apart, with a longer mark every ten degrees.

docs.title: Reading the route
docs.text:
The ND reads waypoint positions and identifiers from the MSFS flight plan. With at least two waypoints, a magenta line joins them in flight-plan order. To see the route on a first flight, set a departure and destination in the simulator before entering the cockpit. Pick two familiar airports close enough to fit on the same map scale.

The box at the top always refers to helicopter heading. A route leg can run across the screen at a different angle, particularly before you turn to join it. In heading-up orientation, the aircraft symbol points up while the route rotates as you turn. In north-up orientation, the route holds its orientation and the aircraft symbol turns instead.

docs.title: When the map looks empty
docs.text:
• Heading and aircraft symbol visible, no terrain picture. The V5.2.4 ND draws its compass and route on a plain background. A chart image is not part of this display format.
  • One waypoint visible, no magenta line. The display needs two waypoint positions to draw the first leg.
  • Route missing after editing the flight plan. Check the departure and destination in MSFS. The display reads the plan when its instrument loads. If you're trying to isolate a route issue, start a new flight with the plan already selected.

The RA readout at the right follows the same height ranges as the one on the primary flight display.

V5.2.4 instrument reference

docs.title: Primary Flight Display
docs.text:
Select PFD on the bottom bezel. Use the horizon in the center to read pitch and bank. The heading scale shows which way the nose is pointing. The airspeed indicator is on the left, with altitude and vertical speed on the right.

Indication How to read it KTS Indicated airspeed in knots. A headwind can give you airspeed while your position over the ground changes very little. Heading The boxed number shows current gyro heading in degrees. With the flight director active, HDG and its bug show the selected heading separately. FEET Indicated barometric altitude. The adjacent IN readout gives the pressure setting in inches of mercury. Vertical speed The scale extends above and below zero. Read direction from the pointer and the rate in feet per minute. The digital number shows the magnitude for both a climb and a descent.

docs.title: Low-speed indication
docs.text: In V5.2.4 the digital airspeed window bottoms out at 30. It can still read 30 while the helicopter is sitting on the ramp. For a check in the simulator, watch the scenery or your movement on the navigation display to see how quickly you're traveling over the ground.

docs.title: Heading selection
docs.text:
Compare the current heading with the selected heading when reading the compass. For example, a current heading of 085 and a selected heading of 100 place the bug to the right of the nose. FD1 appears when the flight director is active. The heading bug marks a reference and can move while the helicopter is stationary.

V5.2.4 instrument reference

docs.title: Airspeed References and Route Timing
docs.text:
Three speed readings answer different questions during a cross-country flight.

Reading Unit Use in the sim Indicated airspeed KIAS Read it on the cockpit airspeed scale and compare it with indicated-speed markings. True airspeed KTAS Use it for motion through the airmass. At altitude, true and indicated airspeed can differ. Groundspeed kt Use it with remaining track distance in nautical miles to calculate an arrival time.

In Delta's V5.2.4 flight model the cruise reference is 100 KTAS and the maximum indicated speed field is 140 KIAS. Microsoft uses reference-speed fields for features such as aircraft selection and speed indications. These entries describe the add-on configuration. A published cruise reference alone cannot predict your groundspeed or fuel burn.

docs.title: Time a leg with the wind
docs.text:
Suppose a leg is 60 NM long. For a simple estimate, use 100 KTAS and assume the wind is directly along the route. With a crosswind, use the actual groundspeed along your planned track.

Wind component Estimated groundspeed Time for 60 NM Calm 100 kt 36 min 20 kt headwind 80 kt 45 min 20 kt tailwind 120 kt 30 min

The calculation is minutes = 60 × distance in NM ÷ groundspeed in kt. A 60 NM outbound leg at 80 kt followed by a 60 NM return at 120 kt takes 75 minutes altogether. Averaging the two speeds gives 100 kt and a 72-minute estimate, which comes up short because the slower leg takes longer.

Once in cruise, recalculate from the distance still to go and the groundspeed you actually see. If 24 NM remain at 80 kt, the new estimate is 18 minutes. Add time for anything the distance-to-destination readout doesn't include, such as an arrival circuit or a stop along the way. For fuel planning, apply the measured total burn in your own simulator to each leg's elapsed time.

H-60 flight model · Flight model reference fields

docs.title: Cabin Loading and Center of Gravity
Cabin Loading and Center of Gravity
docs.text: Gross weight tells you how much the rotor must support. Center of gravity (CG) tells you where that weight acts. Move a load between two stations and the total stays the same, while the balance changes. This is useful when two saved flights show the same weight but need different amounts of cyclic to hold the same attitude.

docs.title: Station positions
docs.text:
These offsets are from the stock UH-60M flight model in V5.2.4. Forward and right are positive in the simulator's coordinate system. The datum is an imaginary reference point set by the model developer. These figures apply to the simulator's loading stations.

Station Fore/aft arm Left/right arm Pilot +6.5 ft −2.3 ft Copilot +6.5 ft +2.3 ft Gunner Left +1.6 ft −2.0 ft Gunner Right +1.7 ft +2.0 ft CARGO −6.0 ft 0 ft

Adding weight to CARGO moves the CG toward that aft station. Splitting an equal load between the two forward seats cancels their left/right moments because their lateral arms are equal and opposite.

docs.title: Same weight, different balance
docs.text:
Try two loadouts at the same fuel quantity. In the first, leave the copilot seat empty and put at least 150 lb in CARGO. In the second, subtract 150 lb from CARGO and enter 150 lb at the copilot station. The weight has moved 12.5 ft forward and 2.3 ft right in the model.

For an aircraft weighing exactly 15,000 lb in this example:

Change Calculation CG shift Fore/aft 150 lb × 12.5 ft ÷ 15,000 lb 0.125 ft, or 1.5 in forward Left/right 150 lb × 2.3 ft ÷ 15,000 lb 0.023 ft, or 0.28 in right

The movement can be too small to see on a coarse CG graphic. Check the station totals and the direction of the change before judging it by helicopter attitude. Compare loadouts with the same wind, fuel and controller trim. A steady wind or an off-center input can otherwise feel like a loading difference.

H-60 flight model · Flight model reference fields

docs.title: Fuel Load and Cruise Endurance
docs.text:
Delta's V5.2.4 UH-60M flight model defines two 180 US gal main tanks. With both at the same percentage, 100% is 360 US gal total, 50% is 180 US gal total and 25% is 90 US gal total. Read both tank quantities when one has been edited independently. A half-full left tank and an empty right tank hold only 90 US gal between them.

Use the same units for fuel on board and fuel burn. If the fuel quantity is in pounds, use pounds per hour. If you take the quantity in gallons, measure gallons per hour. When a display gives a separate flow for each engine, add both flows before calculating endurance.

docs.title: Measure cruise burn in your copy of the sim
docs.text:
1. Choose a repeatable cruise condition. Record variant, gross weight, altitude and airspeed so you can use the result on a similar flight.
  2. Once established in cruise, write down total fuel and simulation time. Repeat the reading after ten or more simulated minutes. Start and end the sample in level flight.
  3. Subtract the second reading from the first. Multiply by 60, then divide by the elapsed minutes. A ten-minute sample uses a multiplier of six.
  4. Keep a separate allowance for start, hover, climb and the ground time you expect on this flight. If the quantity never changes, check unlimited-fuel assistance or whether fuel was added during the sample.

docs.title: Example fuel log
docs.text:
These are sample readings for the arithmetic. Use your own measured burn for a flight plan.

Item Example Total fuel at the start of a 12-minute cruise sample 1,320 lb Total fuel at the end 1,200 lb Measured burn (1,320 − 1,200) × 60 ÷ 12 = 600 lb/h Fuel remaining at the end of the sample 1,200 lb Fuel set aside by the simmer for arrival and reserve 300 lb Fuel available for the remaining cruise 900 lb Remaining cruise time at the sample rate 900 ÷ 600 = 1 h 30 min

At a groundspeed of 90 kt, 1.5 hours gives 135 NM in those steady conditions. At 75 kt the same fuel gives about 113 NM. A headwind may leave endurance almost unchanged at a given power setting while shortening the distance you can cover. Update the estimate when the groundspeed, load or fuel flow changes.

docs.title: Gross Weight and Payload Stations
docs.text: The stock UH-60M 20743 in Delta Simulations V5.2.4 starts from a configured empty weight of 12,511 lb. Its flight model lists 23,000 lb as the maximum gross weight. The difference, 10,489 lb, has to cover everyone on board, cargo and fuel together. Use the loaded weight shown in MSFS for the aircraft in front of you. A saved flight can start with different quantities at every station.

docs.title: The five payload stations
docs.text:
Open the aircraft's fuel and payload settings and read the station weights before changing them. The table gives the defaults in the released flight model.

Station in the model Default load Where the weight goes Pilot 200 lb Forward seat, left side of the model datum Copilot 200 lb Forward seat, right side of the model datum Gunner Left 200 lb Left cabin crew position Gunner Right 200 lb Right cabin crew position CARGO 1,000 lb Aft of the cabin crew, on the centerline

Together these defaults add 1,800 lb. With the tanks empty, that gives 14,311 lb. A station value is a total. To put 350 lb of baggage in a station that currently shows 1,000 lb, enter 350, which removes 650 lb from the aircraft. When changing a visible crew or cabin option, check the station readouts separately.

docs.title: Example load for a short flight
docs.text:
For two occupants and baggage, enter 190 lb for the pilot, 170 lb for the copilot, zero for each cabin crew station and 350 lb for cargo. The five entries total 710 lb. If the sim shows 1,200 lb of fuel, the departure gross weight is:

12,511 + 710 + 1,200 = 14,421 lb.

If MSFS shows a different total, first check whether your fuel is displayed in gallons and whether a station still contains its default load. A common discrepancy in this example is exactly 400 lb from the two occupied cabin crew positions. Once the total agrees, check where the load sits. Two aircraft at the same gross weight can have different centers of gravity.

docs.title: Hover Power and Density Altitude
docs.text: A helicopter close to a flat surface benefits from ground effect. As it climbs clear of that effect, it generally takes more power to hold the same stationary hover. A warmer day, a higher field elevation or a heavier aircraft can also change the power required. You can see how strongly your installed flight model responds by changing one condition at a time.

docs.title: What to record
docs.text:
Use AGL (height above the ground) to describe the hover and MSL (height above mean sea level) to describe the field. At an airport 5,000 ft above sea level, a helicopter can sit on the pad at about 5,000 ft MSL with zero ground clearance. An altimeter reading of 5,000 ft by itself says nothing about ground effect.

For each run, record field elevation, air temperature, pressure setting, wind, starting gross weight and the height being compared. On the engine display, note torque for both engines and the rotor-speed indication once the helicopter has settled. Keep each engine's torque reading separate so you can compare the same indication from one run to the next.

Pair of runs Change Keep the same Low hover / higher hover Height over the same level surface Weather, load, helicopter and location Cool day / warm day Outside air temperature at one field Pressure, wind, weight and hover height Light cabin / heavier cabin Weight at the centerline cargo station Location, weather and hover height

docs.title: Reading the comparison
docs.text:
If torque rises as you leave the surface and rotor speed stays steady, the second hover is using more power. If rotor speed or height changes throughout a run, you are comparing a transition with a hover. Repeat the sample after the height settles.

Density altitude describes the altitude in the standard atmosphere at which air has the same density as the air around the aircraft. Warmer air at the same pressure gives a higher density altitude. Two runs at the same field elevation can therefore give different results. Turn off live weather for this comparison and restore the initial fuel quantity between runs.

A useful entry in your flight notes is “same load, same pad, 10 °C warmer, torque changed by X percentage points.” For example, 64% to 68% is a change of four percentage points. A single pair of sim readings describes those two conditions. Repeat at other loads before using that observation to plan another flight.

docs.title: Aircraft Selection and Tablet Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Start with the symptom you can reproduce. An aircraft missing from the selector, a missing tablet, and a disabled hoist button each point to a different part of the add-on.

Symptom First check What to try next The H-60 is absent from the selector Open the active Community folder from the simulator. Check for deltasimulations-uh60 → manifest.json. Correct any extra folder level, restart MSFS, and search for UH-60. In MSFS 2024, also check My Library → Community and whether the package is enabled. The aircraft loads but the tablet is missing Look for the PEDAL ADJUST click spot. Click once to restore the tablet. If the screen is present but dim, open Settings → EFB BRIGHTNESS. Map is blank while the other tablet tabs work The Map tab loads OpenTopoMap over the internet. Check the provider's availability. The aircraft and settings pages use different data. A tablet or cockpit control will not respond to a mouse click Check the simulator's cockpit interaction mode. Delta designs the controls for Legacy interaction. Try the same control on a stock aircraft variation using the Legacy setting where the simulator offers it. HOIST, PROBE, or BAMBI BUCKET is grey Check the full variation name in the selector. An HH-60M Medevac has a hoist. A civilian Helitak already has a fixed tank, so the separate bucket selector is disabled. A new livery shows the wrong equipment or cabin Load the corresponding included livery and compare the tablet controls. If the stock variant is correct, check which base model and H-60 release the repaint was made for.

docs.title: Reproduce a package problem
docs.text:
Keep the downloaded ZIP, close the simulator, and move the previous H-60 package and third-party H-60 repaints to a backup folder outside Community. Install one fresh copy of the released aircraft and reproduce the issue with a stock variation. Restore the repaints one at a time if that resolves it.

For an issue report, include the H-60 release tag, MSFS edition and build, full aircraft variation, and the steps from loading the flight to seeing the problem. A cockpit screenshot showing the active tablet tab and an exterior screenshot of the selected model make a configuration problem much easier to identify. Use the project's issue tracker or its support Discord.

docs.title: Bambi Bucket and Helitak Tank
docs.text: The H-60 has two firefighting configurations. The Bambi bucket hangs below the aircraft. The Helitak tank is built into the belly of the dedicated civilian Helitak variant. Both use the WATER SYSTEM panel on the aircraft tablet.

docs.title: Select the equipment
docs.text:
To use In the simulator Tablet indication Bambi bucket Select a model without the fixed tank. On Aircraft → CONFIGURATION, select BAMBI BUCKET. BAMBI and a water-level bar. Helitak tank Choose S70i Civilian Helitak N60HD in the aircraft selector. HELITAK and a water-level bar. The bucket selector is disabled on this model. Neither On a model without the fixed tank, turn BAMBI BUCKET off. NO WATER EQUIPMENT.

On the Helitak, the bucket button can look selected even though there is no hanging bucket. Check the HELITAK label on the right. The belly tank already occupies the water-equipment position.

docs.title: Fill and release
docs.text:
1. With the equipment selected, press FORCE FILL. The blue bar and percentage should rise to 100%. This is a convenient way to set up a practice flight or confirm that you have the intended equipment.
  2. Once airborne in the simulator, select DROP. Watch the water percentage fall. Select DROP again to end a partial release. The add-on inhibits discharge while the simulator reports the aircraft is on the ground.
  3. You can also refill over water. The simulation checks the underlying surface, radio height and true airspeed. The bucket and tank have different pickup heights. Crossing a shoreline at cruise speed won't refill either one.
  4. To put the release on your hardware, find DECREASE MAC CREADY in the MSFS controls menu. This is the binding labeled Release Water on the tablet. In the project keybind list the event appears as MAC_CREADY_SETTING_DEC.

If you get the drop control but no effect, check the water percentage first, then confirm that the aircraft is airborne in the sim. If the panel only reads NO WATER EQUIPMENT, return to CONFIGURATION and select the bucket, or reload with the Helitak variant.

docs.title: Cockpit Tablet and Map
docs.text:
The H-60 carries its own cockpit tablet. Click PEDAL ADJUST to hide or show it. With cockpit tooltips enabled, the click spot reads EFB HIDE/SHOW. Use the tabs along the bottom edge of the tablet to change pages.

Tab What it contains Aircraft Crew and door controls, equipment for the selected variant, the water system, and external light controls. Map An embedded OpenTopoMap. It needs an internet connection to load the map tiles. Settings Rotor appearance, custom downwash effects, tablet brightness, and a reference list of hardware bindings.

docs.title: Map behavior
docs.text:
The map opens at a preset location in Kentucky. An aircraft spawned elsewhere can therefore be hundreds of miles from the area on screen. Pan and zoom to explore the area you want. For aircraft navigation, use the navigation display in the cockpit. The tablet map opens an external map location independently of the aircraft position and active flight plan.

If only Map is blank, switch back to Aircraft. Working door and equipment controls indicate that the tablet itself is running. Check internet access to the map provider before reinstalling the H-60.

docs.title: Screen and rotor settings
docs.text:
On Settings, the EFB BRIGHTNESS slider runs from 0% to 100%. Change it here if the tablet is hard to read. If the mount and tablet have disappeared together, use the PEDAL ADJUST click spot first.

Under VISUAL CONFIGURATION, ROTOR TYPE switches between MESH and BLURRED. Change the setting and compare the rotor from the same external camera angle. CUSTOM DOWNWASH FX has its own on/off setting, so you can compare the two rotor styles without changing the downwash effect.

The keybindings listed on Settings are a reference. To assign one, open the controls menu in MSFS, select the hardware device you intend to use, and edit its active profile.

docs.title: Doors, Crew and External Equipment
docs.text: Use Aircraft on the cockpit tablet to set up the helicopter on the ramp. The top-down drawing sits above DOOR CONFIGURATION. Use the labeled buttons below the drawing, then switch to an outside view to check the result.

docs.title: Cockpit and cabin doors
docs.text:
Tablet control What changes DOOR L Opens or closes the left cockpit door. DOOR R Opens or closes the right cockpit door. HIDE DOORS Hides or restores both front door models. The individual open and closed positions are controlled separately. TROOP DOOR Moves the rear cabin doors. GUNNER WIN Operates the crew window where the variant has a movable window. The HH-60M medical cabin has a sealed section here.

If a front door appears to be missing, restore it with HIDE DOORS before trying DOOR L or DOOR R. If the cabin doors move oddly on an older installation, the V5.2.4 release includes a correction to the troop-door animation.

docs.title: People in the cabin
docs.text:
CREW VISIBILITY has four independent switches: PILOT, CO-PILOT, CREW CHIEF, and TROOPS. Start with an outside view of the front seats when checking pilot visibility. The cockpit camera has separate visibility rules for pilot body parts. For a clear look at the cabin figures, open the troop doors and inspect from the side.

These buttons control character models. Set the simulated crew and cargo weights in the aircraft payload controls. A photograph of an empty cabin tells you nothing about the load entered there.

docs.title: Fittings and equipment
docs.text:
Under CONFIGURATION, SKIS adds or removes the ski models at the landing gear. EIBF controls the engine inlet filter model. Both changes are easiest to see from outside.

The EQUIPMENT panel enables HOIST and PROBE according to the selected variant. On an equipped model, HOIST operates the simulated hoist animation. A dimmed button means the current model has no corresponding fitting. If you want to check the animation on an included aircraft, choose an HH-60M Medevac and use the exterior camera.

docs.title: H-60 Variant Selection
docs.text: Several H-60s share the same aircraft type in the selector. Check the full variation name when choosing a helicopter. The two civilian S-70i entries, for example, carry the same registration but load different equipment.

docs.title: Included utility and rescue aircraft
docs.text:
These are selection labels from the V5.2.4 package. The HOIST and PROBE columns show which equipment controls the model enables on the cockpit tablet.

Variation How to recognize it HOIST PROBE UH-60M 20743 Standard utility Mike with upturned exhausts — — UH-60M 20743 (HIRSS) Alternate exhaust installation on the Mike — — HH-60M Medevac 20946 or HH-60M Medevac 21018 Medical cabin and external rescue hoist Available — HH-60U Ghost Hawk 20321 HH-60U model Available — HH-60W Jolly Green II 14481 HH-60W model with hoist and probe Available Available UH-60M HRT (FBI) 27368 HRT model with hoist Available — S70i Civilian N60HD Civilian model without a fixed firefighting tank — — S70i Civilian Helitak N60HD Civilian model with a fixed belly tank — —

docs.title: Check the equipment after spawning
docs.text:
Open the cockpit tablet's Aircraft tab. On an HH-60M Medevac, HOIST is available and PROBE is dimmed. On the Helitak, WATER SYSTEM identifies the fixed tank as HELITAK. If you loaded an S-70i and see NO WATER EQUIPMENT, check the full variant name before changing the aircraft configuration.

For a medical flight, look into the cabin as well as at the paint. The HH-60M uses a dedicated patient interior and has a sealed section at the crew window. A repaint can look like a rescue helicopter while still using the base utility model. To check whether an unexpected cabin or disabled tablet control comes from the repaint, load one of the stock entries in the table and compare.

docs.title: Installation and Updates
docs.text: The H-60 is a PC add-on. The installable download on the aircraft releases page is deltasimulations-uh60.zip, under Assets. GitHub also offers a source archive for each release. That archive contains the project used to build the aircraft. Choose the named aircraft ZIP for your Community folder.

docs.title: Find the active Community folder
docs.text:
Simulator Where to look MSFS 2024 Open Marketplace → My Library, choose Settings beside the search field, then Open. This opens the active Community folder in File Explorer. MSFS 2020 Enable Developer Mode in the general settings. In the developer toolbar, open Virtual File System → Packages Folders → Open Community Folder.

Opening the folder from the sim is especially useful if you installed packages on another drive or have both simulator versions on the same PC.

docs.title: Install the aircraft
docs.text:
1. Note the release tag on GitHub. Download and extract deltasimulations-uh60.zip.
  2. Open the extracted folder. Find deltasimulations-uh60 with manifest.json and layout.json inside.
  3. Close MSFS. Copy that package folder to the Community folder you opened above.
  4. Check the result in File Explorer. You should be able to open Community\deltasimulations-uh60\manifest.json directly. A second deltasimulations-uh60 folder between those two levels keeps the sim from finding the package.
  5. Launch the simulator and look for UH-60 in the aircraft selector. In MSFS 2024 you can also select the Community filter in My Library to check whether the sim recognized the package.

docs.title: Update an existing installation
docs.text:
With MSFS closed, move the previous H-60 package outside Community before copying the new one in. Keeping a backup elsewhere lets you return to the older build and keeps obsolete files out of the updated aircraft. For the first flight after an update, select one of the included liveries. If it loads correctly, try your usual repaint.

If you use a development build, record its commit or archive date. For a release build, keep the GitHub tag. A report that identifies both the H-60 build and the MSFS version is easier to reproduce.

docs.title: Apron and Airborne Start States
docs.text:
Where you begin a flight changes the systems you inherit. The H-60 package defines an apron preset for a parked start and a cruise preset for an airborne start. Use the same start type when comparing two installations or trying to reproduce a cockpit issue.

What to look at Apron preset Cruise preset Main batteries Both overhead battery switches off. Both on, with the standby instrument battery armed. Engines Both at zero RPM with the starter switches off. Running, with both power control levers at the top of their travel and both engine generator switches on. Navigation sensors EGI 1 and EGI 2 off. EGI 1 and EGI 2 on. Flight controls Both SAS channels, FPS and trim off. Flight initialization selects both SAS channels, FPS and trim. Brakes and displays Parking brake set. The helicopter can start with dark screens. Display power buttons selected on.

docs.title: A dark panel on the ramp
docs.text: First look at the battery switches and the engine indications. If you selected a parking position, a quiet aircraft with its batteries off matches the apron preset. Follow Before Start and Cockpit Equipment Checks from there. An airborne start has already selected several of those switches. Repeating every toggle from memory can turn a system back off.

docs.title: Comparing two sessions
docs.text:
For a repeatable comparison, use the same aircraft variant, airport, starting position and fuel load. Before touching a switch, capture the overhead panel and the MFDs. For an electrical issue, include the battery and generator positions. For an engine issue, include both power control levers and the numbered EICAS messages. Record whether the session began parked, in the air or from a saved flight. Those details help distinguish a difference in starting state from a switch that fails to respond.

V5.2.4 aircraft systems

docs.title: Auxiliary Power Unit
docs.text:
The APU can supply electricity to the parked helicopter and bleed air for engine start. The overhead panel gives you separate controls for the APU itself, its generator, its fuel pump and the air source. That distinction matters when you can hear the APU but the cockpit still looks dark.

Overhead control What it does in the sim APU CONT Starts or stops the APU. The cockpit tooltip reads APU CNTRL. FUEL PUMP The APU BOOST position selects the APU's electric fuel pump. Its tooltip reads PRIME APU. This is a separate pump from the two engine boost pumps. GENERATORS APU Connects the APU generator when the unit can supply power. Its tooltip reads APU GEN. AIR SCE HT/STRT Selects the bleed-air source. The cockpit tooltips identify ENGINE, OFF and APU.

docs.title: APU indications
docs.text:
Watch the overhead APU ON light as the unit spools up. Once EICAS is available, look for APU ON in the advisory box. The overhead light comes on slightly earlier than the EICAS message in this build. APU GEN ON is a second advisory. It appears when MSFS reports that the generator is active.

If you see APU ON by itself, check the APU generator switch. Changing the air source selects bleed air. It will not bring a generator online. If you see both advisories but one MFD stays dark, check the power button on that screen. Each display has its own.

docs.title: APU fuel supply
docs.text:
The add-on draws APU fuel from the left main tank. If the APU will not start after you edit the fuel load in MSFS, check the left tank individually. The aircraft can show fuel in TOTAL with all of that fuel in the right tank. The APU needs fuel on its own side and electrical power for its starter and pump.

Use the Cockpit Equipment Checks for the normal parked startup sequence.

V5.2.4 aircraft systems

docs.title: Batteries, Generators and Display Power
docs.text:
The add-on models three electrical buses. Both main batteries, both engine generators, the APU generator and external power connect to the hot battery bus. That bus connects to the main and essential avionics buses. The standby instrument battery has its own connection to the essential avionics bus.

Bus Examples in the add-on Main The general panel, radios, engine starter controls, electric fuel pumps and most lighting circuits. Hot battery Connection point for the main batteries, generators and external power. Essential avionics The standby instrument circuit and standby battery.

docs.title: Operating the overhead switches
docs.text:
The battery and generator controls have separate mouse targets for the normal position and the momentary test position. With tooltips enabled you may see the same switch name over both targets. The test target shows an up-arrow cursor and springs back when released. The normal target shows a down-arrow cursor. For a battery check, hold the test position while you look for BATT GOOD or BATT LOW. To power the cockpit, select the normal ON position.

BATT STBY INST arms a separate supply. The add-on brings this battery online when the main bus loses power. The two engine generators have individual switches, ENG1 GEN and ENG2 GEN. EICAS can report GEN 1 FAIL or GEN 2 FAIL if that generator is switched off or its output is low. Seeing these messages with the engines stopped is consistent with the starting state.

docs.title: One MFD is on and another is dark
docs.text:
Each MFD has its own power button. In version 5.2.4, MFD 2 can power up at a lower main-bus voltage than MFDs 1 and 3. One lit display on battery power can therefore be normal. Once the APU or engine generators are supplying power, check the power button on each remaining display.

APU GEN ON confirms that the APU generator is active. EXT PWR CONNECTED reports the simulator's external power state. If you're comparing starts at different parking spots, note which of those advisories you have before changing any settings.

V5.2.4 aircraft systems

docs.title: Engine Power Control Levers
docs.text: Each engine has a power control lever (PCL) overhead. In the virtual cockpit, the lever handle and the cutoff catch are two different mouse targets. This is usually the reason a lever seems stuck at the bottom of its travel.

docs.title: Moving a lever with the mouse
docs.text:
1. In a parked aircraft, move the cursor over the cutoff catch for the engine you want. Look for the PCL CUTOFF tooltip.
  2. Click the catch to move the lever out of cutoff and into the bottom of its working range.
  3. Move the cursor onto the lever handle. Click and drag the handle along its working range. The drag interaction uses sideways mouse movement.
  4. To select cutoff again during shutdown, drag the handle back to the bottom of its range, then click the catch. The catch only changes position at the bottom.

Each lever moves independently. If engine 2's lever stays put while engine 1's moves, select the catch and handle on the engine 2 side. The fuel selectors beside the levers use a different interaction and show ENG1 FUEL or ENG2 FUEL in their tooltips.

docs.title: Reading the engine side correctly
docs.text:
The ignition key controls master ignition. The two starter buttons control individual starters. EICAS can show ENG 1 STARTER ON or ENG 2 STARTER ON according to the starter active in MSFS. A starter indication tells you which starter is engaged. It does not by itself confirm combustion or that a generator is supplying the aircraft.

In version 5.2.4, both sets of EICAS engine tapes take several readings from engine 1, including torque, gas-generator speed and oil pressure. Identical tape readings therefore cannot establish that both engines are running. The starter and engine oil messages have separate inputs for each engine. If you're reporting an issue on one side, include the lever position and the numbered messages along with a screenshot of the tapes.

The Starting Engines checklist gives the normal start and runup flow for the add-on.

V5.2.4 aircraft systems

docs.title: Hydraulic Leak Test Indications
docs.text: The overhead HYD LEAK TEST switch lets you exercise a group of hydraulic messages on EICAS while parked. It has three positions, TEST, NORM and RESET. The add-on registers a new test when MSFS reports that the helicopter is on the ground.

docs.title: What the display shows
docs.text:
EICAS area Messages produced by the test Upper left and upper right RSVR 1 LOW and RSVR 2 LOW Left caution area T/R SERVO 1 FAIL and BACKUP RSVR LOW Advisory box BACK UP PUMP ON and T/R SERVO 2 ON

RSVR refers to a reservoir and T/R to the tail rotor. The number belongs to the system named on that line. For example, RSVR 2 LOW refers to reservoir 2, while T/R SERVO 2 ON refers to the second tail rotor servo. More than one advisory page can be active when the aircraft also has electrical, lighting or fuel pump advisories.

docs.title: Why messages stay up at NORM
docs.text:
In the parked cockpit, selecting TEST sets the test state. Moving the switch back to NORM leaves that state latched. Select RESET to clear the test, then return the switch to NORM. The group of test messages should disappear together. A generator or engine oil message that remains belongs to a different system.

This difference is useful when troubleshooting a saved session. If both reservoir cautions and the two tail rotor servo messages appear together after you've used the switch, check the test state first. The add-on generates that group from a single test input. The messages alone do not establish that MSFS has simulated fluid loss in multiple systems.

V5.2.4 aircraft systems

docs.title: Main Fuel Tanks and Boost Pumps
Main Fuel Tanks and Boost Pumps
docs.text: The two main tanks have separate quantity indications. On EICAS, 1 is the left tank and 2 is the right tank. TOTAL is the fuel weight MSFS reports for the aircraft. The fuel figures on this page are in pounds.

docs.title: Reading the quantities
docs.text:
The display rounds each tank down to the nearest five pounds and does the same to the total. For example, if MSFS contains 208 pounds on the left and 209 on the right, the individual indications read 205 and 205, while TOTAL reads 415. The difference comes from rounding each number separately.

The colored bars have a maximum height. At higher loads you can change the quantity in the fuel menu and see the number change while the bar stays full. Read the figures when comparing the two sides. FUEL 1 LOW and FUEL 2 LOW are driven by the weight in the respective tanks. Adding fuel only to the right tank will not clear a left-tank quantity caution.

docs.title: Fuel controls on the overhead panel
docs.text:
Control How to recognize it What it controls Engine fuel selectors Tooltips include ENG1 FUEL or ENG2 FUEL, followed by OFF, DIR or XFD. The selected engine's feed setting. DIR means direct feed and XFD means crossfeed. Engine boost pumps Two switches with ENG1 BOOST PUMP and ENG2 BOOST PUMP tooltips. Individual electric pumps. EICAS reports their switch states as BOOST PUMP 1 ON and BOOST PUMP 2 ON. APU boost A separate three-position fuel pump selector with a PRIME APU tooltip in its APU position. The APU pump on the left main tank's supply line.

An engine boost-pump advisory tells you the switch is on. Quantity is a separate indication, and neither boost-pump switch transfers fuel to the other tank. If you're trying to reproduce a fuel problem in the sim, note the left and right quantities, each selector position and the numbered boost-pump advisories. Two aircraft with the same TOTAL can have very different fuel distributions.

V5.2.4 aircraft systems
